abstract: Watermarking is a technique for embedding data within images or audio and is best known in copyright protection. This paper explains how watermarking can be used to embed a unique material identifier (UMID) into every frame of video material to enable tracking throughout the production chain. As the UMID is embedded into the image itself it cannot be separated and then lost. It is embedded at the point of acquisition and enables linking of video material to its associated metadata for rights tracking, technical information, or added-value data services in digital broadcasting. In order to allow a change of UMID, the watermark may be removed or “washed” and a new UMID embedded with no significant generation loss.

authors.bio: Jason Pelly received a B.A. and an M.Sc. in mathematics from the University of Oxford in 1996 and 1997, respectively. In 1999 he joined Sony Broadcast and Professional Europe, in Basingstoke, U.K., and is currently a senior engineer, developing watermarking and digital rights management technologies. While working for Sony, Pelly has been involved with several data compression algorithms, including a studio profile for MPEG-4.

authors.bio: Daniel Tapson received an M.Phys. in mathematics and physics from the University of Warwick, U.K., in 1999. After graduating, he joined Sony Broadcast and Professional Europe, where he currently works as a R&D engineer. During his time at Sony, Tapson has worked on watermarking and other metadata-related projects.

authors.bio: John Stone received a B.Sc. in electrical engineering from Wits University, South Africa, in 1983, and an M.Sc. in communications and signal processing from Imperial College, London, in 1986. He has worked for Sony Broadcast and Professional Europe for the last 11 years. During this time Stone has worked closely in the development of algorithms and architectures for video compression and image processing. — Stone has also been involved with the hardware realization of these systems through VLSI technology. Since 1999 he has led a number of R&D activities including watermarking, video effects, and compression. He holds 28 patents.
